To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the main risk factors for increased patient delay are non-recognition of the seriousness of symptoms, fear of cancer and sanctioning of help-seeking by others, and that the main risk factor for increased practitioner delay is misdiagnosis.

(a) the most important patient-mediated factors that result in delayed presentation of symptomatic cancers are: non-recognition of the seriousness of the symptoms; fear of cancer; and the sanctioning of help-seeking by others; (b) the main practitioner-mediated factors resulting in delayed presentation are: ‘misdiagnosis’, inadequate examination, inappropriate tests and failure to follow-up negative/inconclusive test results; and (c) there is evidence of an association with delayed presentation of: (i) older

(1) patient-mediated delays are more common in patients with less education, less social support, lower income and older age and (2) practitioner-mediated delays are common, and are associated with misdiagnosis and failure to follow up negative/inconclusive investigations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the patient and practitioner journey from the first appearance of a symptom to the time of diagnosis.
identifying factors which may influence the time to presentation of cancer.
the factors that contribute to delayed presentation, and the factors that contribute towards the earlier diagnosis of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk factors for delayed presentation vary by cancer site, and that there is a need to identify and address the factors that may contribute to delayed presentation and referral.
patient delay is the result of a complex interplay of factors, which are not the same across cancer sites.
there is a need to raise awareness of cancer symptoms and to ensure that the health services are responsive to these symptoms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk factors for delayed presentation are similar to those for late diagnosis.

there is a need for more effective communication of the importance of symptoms, particularly for those at high risk, and for more effective communication between patients and practitioners to facilitate timely presentation and referral.
there are many factors influencing patient delay, but the main one is non-recognition of symptoms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to educate the public about the seriousness of cancer symptoms, and to educate health professionals about how to recognise and respond to cancer symptoms.
patients should not be afraid of cancer, but should seek help for symptoms that worry them.
there are a range of factors that may influence the time to cancer diagnosis, and that these factors are likely to differ between cancer sites.
